mcqs.question: Why can a database allow many transactions to hold a shared (S) lock on the same row at once, but only one transaction to hold an exclusive (X) lock?
options: Concurrent reads of the same value can't produce a conflict, but a write must be isolated from every other read or write until it completes
Shared locks are only a logging convention and don't actually block anything
Exclusive locks are deprecated in favor of shared locks in modern engines
The database can't tell the difference between a read and a write, so it defaults to allowing only one lock holder for safety
mcqs.explanation: Multiple readers observing the same committed value creates no conflict, so shared locks can co-exist. A write changes the value, so it must exclude every other reader and writer until it's done — that's the whole reason exclusive locks exist. Shared locks do block exclusive locks, and engines absolutely distinguish reads from writes.

mcqs.question: A transaction releases a shared lock on row X mid-transaction (plain 2PL, not strict), and another transaction then reads X and proceeds based on that value. The first transaction later aborts. What problem does this illustrate, and what fixes it?
options: This is a deadlock; the fix is lock escalation
This is a phantom read; the fix is a next-key lock
This is write skew; the fix is Serializable isolation
This is a dirty-read-like cascading dependency; the fix is strict 2PL, which holds all locks until commit
mcqs.explanation: Releasing a lock before commit lets another transaction build on a value that might later be rolled back — a cascading-abort risk similar in shape to a dirty read. Strict 2PL closes this by holding every lock until commit or abort. It isn't a deadlock, phantom, or write-skew scenario.

mcqs.question: A transaction requests an exclusive lock on an entire table that already has 50 rows individually locked by other transactions. How does the engine determine there's a conflict without scanning all 50 row locks?
options: It can't — this always requires a full row-by-row scan of every lock
It checks the table's intention-lock state, which the row-lock holders already registered when they acquired their row locks
It optimistically grants the table lock and rolls back later if a conflict is found
It refuses all table-level locks unconditionally while any row lock exists anywhere in the database
mcqs.explanation: Intention locks exist exactly for this: a transaction taking a row lock first registers an intention lock at the table level, so a later table-level request only has to inspect that summary, not every individual row lock. There's no full scan, no optimistic grant-then-rollback here, and it's not an unconditional refusal.

mcqs.question: A single popular product's inventory row is updated by hundreds of concurrent checkout transactions per second, and overall database throughput has collapsed even though CPU and disk are far from saturated. What's the most likely explanation?
options: Lock contention on that one hot row is serializing transactions that would otherwise run in parallel, so most connections are simply waiting, not working
The database has run out of disk space for new rows
The query planner is choosing a full table scan instead of an index
Replication lag is causing every read to retry
mcqs.explanation: Low CPU and disk usage alongside collapsed throughput is the signature of contention, not a resource shortage: transactions are queued waiting for a lock on the hot row rather than doing real work. Disk space, a bad query plan, or replication lag would show up differently (disk errors, high CPU from scans, or read-side symptoms), not this pattern.

mcqs.question: Under InnoDB's default Repeatable Read, why can an INSERT of a brand-new row block on a completely unrelated-looking UPDATE that only touched existing rows in a different part of the same range?
options: It's a bug specific to InnoDB that Postgres does not share
InnoDB requires an ACCESS EXCLUSIVE lock on the whole table for any UPDATE
The UPDATE's next-key lock included the gap the new row would be inserted into, blocking the INSERT until it commits
MySQL always serializes all writes to a table regardless of isolation level
mcqs.explanation: InnoDB prevents phantoms via gap/next-key locks, which lock the space between index values as well as the values themselves — so an INSERT landing in a locked gap blocks even though it doesn't touch any row the UPDATE explicitly locked. This is intended behavior, not a bug, isn't full-table locking, and Postgres avoids it only because it uses MVCC snapshots instead of gap locks for this.

mcqs.question: A money-transfer function locks the source account row, then the destination account row, in whatever order the caller happened to pass them in. What's the most direct fix to prevent deadlocks from this pattern?
options: Increase the lock timeout so transactions wait longer before giving up
Always sort the account IDs and acquire locks in that same consistent order, regardless of which account initiated the transfer
Switch the isolation level to Read Uncommitted so locks are never held
Add a retry loop that simply re-runs the transaction after any failure
mcqs.explanation: Deadlocks from opposite-order locking are prevented structurally by always acquiring locks in one consistent order (e.g., ascending ID) — the specific cross-wait pattern becomes impossible. A longer timeout or blind retries just delay or mask the problem, and Read Uncommitted removes correctness guarantees without addressing lock ordering at all.
